title: Microplastics Built to Last May Finally Have a Biological Weakness, Scientists Say
excerpt: A comprehensive new review outlines how bacteria, fungi and engineered enzymes could break down the synthetic polymers that filtration and dredging cannot, though major hurdles remain.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A new review highlights biological methods to dismantle synthetic polymers using microbes and enzymes.
  • CRISPR and enzyme engineering have accelerated the degradation of plastics like PET in labs.
  • The microbe X-32 can convert polyethylene and polypropylene into carbon dioxide and water in 22 months.
  • The postbiotic supplement Qi601 can reduce microplastics in human saliva by over 90%.

Applied Microbiology, New Scientist
  • A new scientific review published in Applied Microbiology details how bacteria, fungi, microbial communities and plastic-degrading enzymes could dismantle synthetic polymers at the molecular level.
  • CRISPR-based genome editing and enzyme engineering have improved the stability and activity of plastic-eating enzymes, accelerating PET degradation in laboratory settings.
  • A startup called Breaking has discovered a microbe called X-32 that can fully convert polyethylene and polypropylene — the toughest common plastics — to carbon dioxide and water in 22 months.
  • A separate study found that a postbiotic supplement called Qi601 can bind to and reduce free-floating microplastics in human saliva by over 90 percent.

The Scale of the Problem

Microplastic pollution has become one of the defining environmental challenges of the decade. Tiny fragments of synthetic polymers — smaller than five millimeters and often invisible to the naked eye — have been found in human blood, placentas, brain tissue, drinking water and food. Filtration can capture some particles, dredging can remove contaminated sediment, and chemical treatment can alter certain polymers. But these interventions are expensive, incomplete and often shift the problem from one location to another rather than solving it.

A comprehensive new scientific review, published in the journal Applied Microbiology, argues that the most promising alternative may come from biology itself — organisms too small to see that can colonize plastic surfaces, weaken polymer chains and metabolize the fragments.

Engineering Microbes to Eat Plastic

The review brings together developments across microbial ecology, enzyme engineering, CRISPR gene editing, synthetic biology and bioreactor design. The core finding: scientists can now increasingly engineer biological processes to make them faster and more targeted at specific polymer types.

Recent CRISPR applications, including base editing and promoter modification, have improved the stability and expression of key enzymes such as PETase and cutinase — proteins that can break down polyethylene terephthalate, the plastic used in water bottles and food packaging. Machine learning-based enzyme design is pushing these proteins toward greater thermostability and broader substrate adaptation.

Perhaps the most striking laboratory result comes from a startup called Breaking, which emerged from Harvard's Wyss Institute. The company's scientists discovered a microorganism they call X-32 while prospecting at polluted lakes and Superfund sites. When fed polyethylene and polypropylene — the tough plastics used in packaging that have historically resisted biological attack — X-32 grew, indicating it was digesting the material. Respiratory experiments confirmed the polymers were being fully converted to carbon dioxide and water in 22 months.

"Not only do we want to break down plastics, we don't want to make more microplastics. We really want to eradicate plastics through breaking those chemical bonds."

— Ben Lamm, CEO of Colossal Biosciences and Breaking board member

A Human-Scale Intervention

On the human health front, a separate study published in New Scientist describes a postbiotic supplement called Qi601 that may reduce microplastic exposure inside the body. In laboratory tests, Qi601 — made from dead bacterial cell walls with rough surfaces — spontaneously bound to up to 92 percent of nanoplastics in fluids simulating the digestive system.

When tested in human participants chewing commercial gum, which releases microplastic particles into saliva, the supplement reduced freely floating particles from 2,152 to 185 in one participant's sample. The researchers described it as the first demonstration of a microplastic mitigant working in a human context, though they cautioned that the study has not yet shown the particles were prevented from entering gut cells or excreted from the body.

Challenges and Reality Checks

The review is clear-eyed about the limitations. The hardest plastics — polyethylene and polystyrene — still resist most biological attack under real-world conditions. Laboratory performance often deteriorates when scaled up. Engineered organisms raise biosafety questions that regulators have not yet fully addressed. And any environmental release of genetically modified microbes would need to clear substantial regulatory barriers.

The breakthrough, the authors conclude, will not come from discovering a single organism that eats all plastic. It will come from building controlled biological systems in which microbes, enzymes, bioreactors and waste infrastructure work together — a systems-level engineering challenge that is still years from deployment but advancing faster than many expected.
